A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSPO research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and rendered figures, support reliable comparison and matching of relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic preference-learning experiments and language-model alignment evaluations, including numerical results, ablations, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds training-time measurements, SFT-augmented baseline comparisons, and experiments with larger labeled datasets.

M1.justification: SSPO retains its paired preference loss, KDE threshold estimation, EMA stabilization, pseudo-labeling, and adaptive scheduling. Algorithm 1 changes the unpaired-loss coefficient from 1−m to 1−γt, bringing the pseudocode into agreement with Eq. (12), already present in v1. This repairs documentation rather than establishing a changed underlying method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic word-preference task, general/medical/business training corpora, and AlpacaEval2.0 and MT-Bench evaluations. The added experiments increase labeled-data quantities and introduce controls within existing coverage; they do not add datasets, domains, or distinct task requirements.

E2.justification: Appendix F.1 and Table 10 add evaluated DPO+SFT and SimPO+SFT comparators for Mistral with 1% and 10% UltraFeedback. Giving these baselines the same paired and unpaired data substantially strengthens the comparison design. The original DPO, ORPO, SimPO, KTO, SSRM, and SPA comparator set remains in Table 2.

E3.justification: Reported DSP Business paired-data counts change from 502/5,021 to 125/1,255. Table 8 revises several baseline settings and changes SSPO's 1%-UltraFeedback Llama3 training from two epochs to one and decay rate from 0.01 to 0.005. The learning-rate sweep extends to 1e-9. Added experiments use an SFT coefficient of 1 and increase labeled data to 1,000/10,000 toy pairs and 100% UltraFeedback. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Figure 3 adds an analysis of reward distributions and threshold movement during Mistral training on DSP Business. Appendix F tests whether ordinary SFT on the same unpaired data explains the gains and whether benefits persist with abundant labels. Appendix E adds computational-cost analysis and measurements. The original noise, prior, and scheduler ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Reward-density plots and EMA standard deviations concern the method's reward distributions, not uncertainty estimates for reported performance.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises multiple scores: for example, Llama3 DPO at 10% UltraFeedback changes from 11.0 to 13.0 LC, while SSPO at 1% changes from 15.0/16.1 to 14.8/16.0 LC/WR alongside revised training settings. Tables 9–12 add runtime, SFT-control, and larger-label results, including 32.4 LC for SSPO versus 26.2 for SPA at 100% UltraFeedback. Business responses from DPO, ORPO, and SimPO are also replaced in v1 Table 14 versus v2 Table 18.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds a computational-complexity derivation covering model computation, KDE, EMA, and pseudo-labeling. Section 4.1 newly interprets the threshold equality as selecting a representative within a separating interval. However, Theorem 1 and its Appendix B.1 proof retain their original statements; no replacement proof establishes the revised interpretation.

C1.justification: The abstract changes its data-efficiency example from Llama3-8B-Instruct to Mistral-7B-Instruct. The central contributions—threshold-based semi-supervised preference optimization and reduced dependence on paired feedback—remain unchanged, as does the conclusion.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix B.2 add explanations involving confirmation bias, reward non-stationarity, and cancellation of noisy pseudo-label gradients. Appendix C.1 adds a population-threshold tracking interpretation. Appendix F attributes gains to preference differentiation beyond ordinary SFT and argues for applicability with abundant labels. These substantially expand the mechanism and applicability arguments.

D1.justification: v2 refines existing implementation documentation with separate data-size configurations in Table 8, a KDE grid size of 200, SFT-control objectives and coefficient, and measured runtimes. It corrects Algorithm 1's loss coefficient and changes the code pointer from GitHub to an anonymous repository. Conversely, the SSRM description drops the explicit statement that its reward model was trained using SimPO.

R1.justification: New Appendix D substantially expands positioning against SSRM and SPA through comparisons of data requirements, training procedures, theoretical grounding, and computational efficiency. v2 also adds Arazo et al. on confirmation bias and Tarvainen and Valpola on consistency-based semi-supervised learning. The original related-work sections are largely retained.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section order remain intact. Revisions concentrate on theorem, metric, gradient, and EMA explanations, with new Appendices D–F and relocation of qualitative examples from D to G. Headers change from the ICLR review designation to 'Preprint.' This is a targeted expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds the three-panel reward-distribution Figure 3 and runtime, control, and scaling Tables 9–12. Table 8 is substantially restructured to separate data fractions and SimPO/SSRM configurations, and Table 5 is reformatted. Figures 1–2 retain identical graphics; earlier qualitative Tables 9–15 largely relocate and become Tables 13–19.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical scrutiny and reproducibility through same-data SFT controls, labeled-data scaling, measured runtimes, and the Algorithm 1 correction. The net gain is limited: DPO+SFT nearly matches SSPO in Table 10, without uncertainty estimates supporting the strong causal interpretation. The new interval interpretation leaves the original theorem and proof unchanged, and updated Llama3 scores in Table 2 now disagree with Table 4. These shortcomings temper the useful additions.
